content.heading: 8.2 Affine Independence
content.paragraph: This section continues to explore the relation between linear concepts and affine concepts. Consider first a set of three vectors in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, say $S = \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\textbf{v}_{3} \right\}$. If $S$ is linearly dependent, then one of the vectors is a linear combination of the other two vectors. What happens when one of the vectors is an affine combination of the others? note.paragraph: An indexed set of points $\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is affinely dependent if there exist real numbers $c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$, not all zero, such that
Otherwise, the set is affinely independent.

content.paragraph: An affine combination is a special type of linear combination, and affine dependence is a restricted type of linear dependence. Thus, each affinely dependent set is automatically linearly dependent.

A set $\{\textbf{v}_{1}\}$ of only one point (even the zero vector) must be affinely independent because the required properties of the coefficients $c_{i}$ cannot be satisfied when there is only one coefficient. For $\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1} \right\}$, the first equation in (1) is just $c_{1} = 0$, and yet at least one (the only one) coefficient must be nonzero.

Exercise 21 asks you to show that an indexed set $\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$ is affinely dependent if and only if $\textbf{v}_{1} = \textbf{v}_{2}$. The following theorem handles the general case and shows how the concept of affine dependence is analogous to that of linear dependence. Parts (c) and (d) give useful methods for determining whether a set is affinely dependent. Recall from Section 8.1 that if $\textbf{v}$ is in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, then the vector $\widetilde{\textbf{v}}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n + 1}$ denotes the homogeneous form of $\textbf{v}$.﻿

note.title: Theorem ﻿5﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿5﻿
note.paragraph: Given an indexed set $S = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, with $p \geq 2$, the following statements are logically equivalent. That is, either they are all true statements or they are all false.

list.item: One of the points in S is an affine combination of the other points in S.﻿
The set {v2−v1,…,vp−v1} in ℝn is linearly dependent.
The set {v˜1,…,v˜p} of homogeneous forms in ℝn+1 is linearly dependent.

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: Suppose statement (a) is true, and let $c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$ satisfy (1). By renaming the points if necessary, one may assume that $c_{1} \neq 0$ and divide both equations in (1) by $c_{1}$, so that $1 + (c_{2}/c_{1}) + \cdots + (c_{p}/c_{1}) = 0$ and

Note that the coefficients on the right side of (2) sum to 1. Thus (a) implies (b). Now, suppose that (b) is true. By renaming the points if necessary, one may assume that $\textbf{v}_{1} = c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2} + \cdots + c_{p}\textbf{v}_{p}$, where $c_{2} + \cdots + c_{p} = 1$. Then
and
Not all of $c_{2},\ldots,c_{p}$ can be zero because they sum to $1$. So (b) implies (c).

Next, if (c) is true, then there exist weights $c_{2},\ldots,c_{p}$, not all zero, such that (4) holds. Rewrite (4) as (3) and set $c_{1} = - \text{(}c_{2} + \cdots + c_{p}\text{)}$. Then $c_{1} + \cdots + c_{p} = 0$. Thus, (3) shows that (1) is true. So (c) implies (a), which proves that (a), (b), and (c) are logically equivalent. Finally, (d) is equivalent to (a) because the two equations in (1) are equivalent to the following equation involving the homogeneous forms of the points in $S$:

In statement (c) of Theorem 5, $\textbf{v}_{1}$ could be replaced by any of the other points in the list $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$. Only the notation in the proof would change. So, to test whether a set is affinely dependent, subtract one point in the set from the other points, and check whether the translated set of $p - 1$ points is linearly dependent.

content.paragraph: Barycentric coordinates have both physical and geometric interpretations. They were originally defined by A. F. Moebius in 1827 for a point $\textbf{p}$ inside a triangular region with vertices $\textbf{a}$, $\textbf{b}$, and $\textbf{c}\text{.}$ He wrote that the barycentric coordinates of $\textbf{p}$ are three nonnegative numbers $m_{\textbf{a}}$, $m_{\textbf{b}}$, and $m_{\textbf{c}}$ such that $\textbf{p}$ is the center of mass of a system consisting of the triangle (with no mass) and masses $m_{\textbf{a}}$, $m_{\textbf{b}}$, and $m_{\textbf{c}}$ at the corresponding vertices. The masses are uniquely determined by requiring that their sum be $1$. This view is still useful in physics today.1

content.heading: Barycentric Coordinates in Computer Graphics
content.paragraph: When working with geometric objects in a computer graphics program, a designer may use a “wire-frame” approximation to an object at certain key points in the process of creating a realistic final image. For instance, if the surface of part of an object consists of small flat triangular surfaces, then a graphics program can easily add color, lighting, and shading to each small surface when that information is known only at the vertices. Barycentric coordinates provide the tool for smoothly interpolating the vertex information over the interior of a triangle. The interpolation at a point is simply the linear combination of the vertex values using the barycentric coordinates as weights.

Colors on a computer screen are often described by RGB coordinates. A triple $(r,g,b)$ indicates the amount of each color—red, green, and blue—with the parameters varying from $0$ to $1\text{.}$ For example, pure red is $(1,0,0)$, white is $(1,1,1)$, and black is $(0,0,0)$.﻿

content.paragraph: One of the last steps in preparing a graphics scene for display on a computer screen is to remove “hidden surfaces” that should not be visible on the screen. Imagine the viewing screen as consisting of, say, a million pixels, and consider a ray or “line of sight” from the viewer’s eye through a pixel and into the collection of objects that make up the $3D$ display. The color and other information displayed in the pixel on the screen should come from the object that the ray first intersects. See Figure7. When the objects in the graphics scene are approximated by wire frames with triangular patches, the hidden surface problem can be solved using barycentric coordinates.
